projectDetails.title: Live Ball Data Visualizer for Cricket
projectDetails.imageAlt: Ball trajectory and broadcast overlay in the cricket visualizer.
textBlocks: A live 3D cricket visualizer that turns ball-tracking data into animations for match analysis and broadcast.

modal.title: Live Ball Data Visualizer for Cricket
modal.context: Cloudworx Studio · 2024 · Frontend development · In collaboration with StanceBeam

sections.content: At Cloudworx Studio, a digital twins company, we collaborated with StanceBeam, a company specializing in cricket data collection and analysis, to build a live cricket ball trajectory visualizer. I worked on the application’s frontend for match analysis and broadcast.

sections.caption: Single-ball trajectory and ticker showing the bowler, over, delivery number, and turn angle.
sections.alt: A single ball trajectory with the bowler name, first over, and a 4.3-degree turn angle in the ticker.

sections.content: StanceBeam developed an ML-based system to track a cricket ball during live matches. Our application received trajectory data through an API and turned it into animations. The visualization needed to be compelling for live telecasts and highly accurate, with Leg-Before-Wicket (LBW) decision analysis as its primary use case.
Interface and animation controls

We built the application with React and React Three Fiber. My primary role was developing the 2D interface with Tailwind CSS. Operators could select an innings, choose an animation package, and select an over and individual balls or all balls in that over. They could leave the camera in place or transition to a stump or impact view, and display ball speed or angle before pitching, after pitching, or as an average. Once the scene was set up, pressing the spacebar started the animation.

images.caption: Graphics-package selection: Over Review, Decision Review, Swing Analysis, Pitch Map, Runs by Over, and Camera Adjust, with an innings selector.
images.alt: The menu for selecting an animation package.

images.caption: Over and ball selection, camera-transition options, and speed or angle data before and after pitching or as an average.
images.alt: Controls for selecting ball data and configuring the scene.

sections.content: I worked with the modeling team to align the virtual stadium with the scale of the incoming data. I also collaborated with the Three.js team on callbacks that connected interface actions to the animation system. The camera-adjustment view also let operators align the virtual pitch with reference broadcast footage.

images.caption: Ball tracking for an LBW review.
images.alt: Ball tracking for an LBW review.

images.caption: Front-view LBW review with pitching, impact, wicket contact, and review-decision overlays.
images.alt: Front view of a ball trajectory with pitching outside off, impact marked umpire’s call, and a not-out review decision.

images.caption: Pitch map showing multiple ball trajectories.
images.alt: Pitch map showing multiple ball trajectories.

sections.content: Review graphics and ticker overlays

The graphics packages included unified over reviews, individual-ball swing analysis, pitch maps, runs by over, and LBW decision reviews. The decision-review overlay displayed pitching position, impact, and projected wicket contact alongside the original decision, final decision, and bowling-team review result.
I also designed the 2D ticker overlay and animated it with Tailwind. It identified the bowler and over, with layouts for per-ball speeds across an over or the turn angle of an individual delivery.

sections.caption: Over-review ticker showing the bowler, over, and speed of each delivery.
sections.alt: Multiple ball trajectories with an orange ticker listing six ball speeds.

sections.content: Camera perspective alignment tool

We made a camera perspective alignment tool that superimposed the virtual pitch over reference broadcast footage. Operators could adjust the field of view, camera position and target, and the reference image’s opacity. Camera configurations could be downloaded and uploaded for reuse.

sections.caption: Demonstration of the camera perspective alignment tool, matching the virtual pitch to a reference broadcast frame.

sections.content: Live broadcast
The application was used in the 2024 Madhya Pradesh Premier League and broadcast live on Jio Cinema.

sections.caption: Live-broadcast excerpt from the 2024 Madhya Pradesh Premier League, showing an LBW review in the match coverage.

modal.introHeading: From ball tracking to live broadcast.

modal.title: 3D Walkthrough Application for Real Estate
modal.context: Personal project · Started in 2020 · Development documented through 2025

sections.content: This project began in 2020 with a question: could we experience the SketchUp models made by interior design students in VR?

sections.caption: A browser-based architectural walkthrough with baked lighting.
sections.alt: A browser-based architectural walkthrough with baked lighting.

sections.content: I wanted people to explore architectural models in an immersive, navigable space that was easy to share and available across devices. A browser-based experience made sense because it did not require specialized software or local installation.
Making the models work on the web

Early SketchUp models were highly detailed and too heavy to render smoothly. I explored reducing polygon counts and optimizing the lighting. The first versions ran on PCs and VR headsets; later, I added touchscreen-friendly navigation for mobile devices.

images.caption: Dining and living spaces in the walkthrough.
images.alt: Dining and living spaces in the walkthrough.

images.caption: A bedroom scene with light and shadows baked into the textures.
images.alt: A bedroom scene with light and shadows baked into the textures.

sections.content: Texture baking

Piyush Jain and I explored baking light and shadows directly into textures. This reduced the need for real-time lighting and helped us balance visual quality with performance. We iterated on the baked lighting across several versions of the environment.
Texture baking was also time-consuming and highly manual. In the 2025 portfolio, I identified automating this workflow with AI as a direction for further exploration.

projectDetails.title: Training Simulation Application for the Logistics Industry
projectDetails.imageAlt: The warehouse training simulation with box handling and a scanner interface.
textBlocks: A browser-based warehouse training simulation with scanning, box handling, and customizable exercises.

modal.title: Training Simulation Application for the Logistics Industry

sections.content: During my sixth-semester internship at Hoansi Studios, I developed a browser-based warehouse training prototype for the logistics industry.

sections.caption: The warehouse training simulation with box handling and a scanner interface.
sections.alt: The warehouse training simulation with box handling and a scanner interface.

sections.content: The training problem

The client worked in the logistics industry in the United States. During COVID-19 restrictions, limits on warehouse staffing meant training new workers on the floor could reduce productivity. Their goal was a virtual module that could shorten a training period of approximately four weeks or eventually replace the need for on-site training. This was the prototype’s aim, rather than a measured result.

The requirements were an immersive 3D environment, interaction with warehouse equipment, real-time instructions and feedback, customizable task sequences, and access through a browser without local installation.
From A-Frame to Three.js

I first built the receiving workflow in A-Frame to test movement and scanning interactions. That version distinguished between pallets and individual boxes, a distinction omitted from later iterations. I then modeled a warehouse in Autodesk Fusion 360 and made its textures and floor markings in Photoshop and Illustrator.

images.caption: The early A-Frame proof of concept.
images.alt: The early A-Frame proof of concept.

images.caption: Warehouse modeling and layout.
images.alt: Warehouse modeling and layout.

sections.content: With the model ready, I moved development to Three.js. I added gaze-based box dragging and dropping, text input for the scanner, and interactions that simulated the receiving workflow.
Configuring an exercise

The setup editor lets an instructor add or remove the printer step, set the number of boxes and their drop-off points, and choose which boxes produce a scan error. A scan error prompts the trainee to enter the information manually.

sections.caption: The setup editor for configuring a training exercise.
sections.alt: The setup editor for configuring a training exercise.

modal.introHeading: Learning the warehouse workflow in a browser.

sections.content: Inspired by my own journey into coding with p5.js, I introduced programming through direct visual feedback. Students explored Cartesian geometry, loops, and randomness, and learned to think algorithmically about composition: instead of only making a final image, they designed rules and systems that generated evolving visuals.

projectDetails.title: Fare Calculation Algorithm Simulator
projectDetails.imageAlt: The fare simulator with a map, configurable rates, and running metrics.
textBlocks: A simulator exploring how fuel costs and fare rules affect auto-rickshaw drivers’ earnings.

modal.title: Fare Calculation Algorithm Simulator

sections.content: For my 2021 pre-thesis project, I researched auto-rickshaw drivers in Bangalore and prototyped a simulator for exploring fare calculation models.

sections.caption: The fare simulator with a map, configurable rates, and running metrics.
sections.alt: The fare simulator with a map, configurable rates, and running metrics.

sections.content: Algorithms and everyday work

Service aggregation apps use algorithms to assign work and calculate pay. Small changes to these systems can have significant effects on the daily lives of gig workers. I wanted to understand those effects in the context of auto-rickshaw drivers.

Coming from Mumbai, where meter regulations were strictly enforced, I found the situation in Bangalore very different. I interviewed 20 drivers from different parts of Bangalore, often with a translator, to understand their perspectives on fares and ride-sharing platforms.
The prototype

The simulator models auto-rickshaws picking up and dropping off passengers within a fixed area. Users can configure fuel cost, the per-kilometer rate, base fare, and minimum distance. As it runs, the interface tracks average fare, take-home earnings, and fuel expenses. I integrated the Google Maps API to ground the simulation in a real map.
What the research revealed

Mathematical optimization can suggest an ideal fare model, but interviews showed that social and political factors often diverge from purely numerical solutions. The project helped me examine where a simulation can be useful and where lived experience complicates its assumptions.

modal.introHeading: Making the economics of a ride visible.

modal.title: Plastic Sweeper — Live Interactive Data Visualization
modal.context: Third-semester studio · 2019 · Featured in the p5.js 2020 showcase

sections.content: Plastic Sweeper is a Minesweeper-inspired game I made in a 2019 studio led by Garret Lynch to communicate the scale of plastic pollution in the oceans.

sections.caption: Plastic Sweeper: an ocean pollution visualization inspired by Minesweeper.
sections.alt: Plastic Sweeper: an ocean pollution visualization inspired by Minesweeper.

sections.content: The studio brief was to create a visualization that responded to real-time data. I chose ocean plastic waste and looked for an interaction that could make its scale tangible.

Players try to uncover the blue tiles while avoiding the red ones. The twist is that the number of red tiles is set by the amount of plastic waste in the oceans. With the data updating live, the increasing difficulty becomes part of the message.
Rubaan Singh created the tile illustrations. Plastic Sweeper was featured in the p5.js 2020 showcase as one of three selected projects from India.

sections.alt: Plastic Sweeper in the p5.js 2020 showcase.

sections.content: I use Fourier transforms to analyze audio and explore sound visualization in Three.js.

sections.caption: A Three.js sound visualization driven by frequency data.
sections.alt: A Three.js sound visualization driven by frequency data.

sections.content: Fourier transforms extract frequency data from an audio file. I use that data to change visual parameters in Three.js, making the elements on screen respond to the sound in real time.
